body.text: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around Wrecks of Saint-Pierre harbor. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts from daily noise.

The wrecks in Saint-Pierre harbor are ships that, except for the Dahlia, were all sunk during the eruption of Mount Pelée on May 8, 1902. The eruption generated a pyroclastic flow (in French nuée ardente, "burning cloud") that destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, Martinique in a few minutes.
During this eruption, it was estimated that 394 boats were in Saint-Pierre's bay, Martinique.

The disappearance of the port administration's archives has made it impossible to draw up an exhaustive list of the shipwrecks caused by the disaster. A report published in 1904 by the Établissement national des invalides de la marine (the French seamen's pension fund) was based on statistics and testimonies.
It estimates the French losses at a minimum of 386 ships and boats, mainly coastal vessels and fishing boats, 500 crew members and 33 passengers.

The foreign losses are at least 3 English ocean-going steamers with 99 crew members, 2 American sailing ships with 20 crew members, 3 Italian ocean-going sailing ships with 28 crew members and one passenger. Like the town, the ships were destroyed in an instant, most caught fire and were lost with all hands.

Local fishermen knew the locations of some of the wrecks, which sometimes snagged their nets and lay in areas rich in fish. With the advent of scuba diving in the 1970s, wreck hunters set out to search for the sunken boats.

Michel Météry and Jean Bally are known as the discoverers of most of these wrecks. The discoveries began in February 1974. Michel Météry and Jean Bally declared all the wrecks to the regional cultural affairs directorate (DRAC) in May 1977.
Jacques Cousteau, Albert Falco and Dominique Serafini on the Calypso were also among those who searched for them.

The wrecks are now very popular dive sites, and all local diving clubs organize trips to them. The Roraima, by its size and state of preservation, is the most emblematic of these wrecks. The Tamaya is less popular because it is too deep for air diving. The Grappler with its "treasure" is still sought after.
More than a century after they sank, the wrecks have become artificial reefs, colonised by marine life, and are among the richest and most diverse in Martinique.
To preserve these cultural and heritage assets of Martinique, in 2012, the city of Saint-Pierre and the French state made the decision to protect the wrecks resting in Saint-Pierre's harbor.
Perret Museum of Saint-Pierre recently launched a podcast in French dedicated to the wrecks.

It features, in alphabetical order, Mathurin Cadenet, originally from Saint-Pierre (nicknamed "Pierrotin"), Daniel Eustache, also Pierrotin and fisherman, Jean-Sébastien France, diver and president of the Association for Research and Valorization of the Archaeological Heritage of Martinique (ARVPAM), and Michel Météry, diver and discoverer of the wrecks in the harbor of Saint-Pierre.
The wrecks are not only important archaeological sites, but also places of remembrance of the tragic events of the 1902 eruption.
Background

At the turn of the 20th century, Saint-Pierre was the largest town in Martinique and one of the most prosperous in the Caribbean. Nicknamed the "Paris of the Antilles", it had about 30,000 inhabitants and concentrated most of the island's economic and cultural life.
Its harbor, sheltered by the volcanic relief, was one of the busiest in the region: merchant ships loaded and unloaded rum, sugar, cocoa and manufactured goods bound for Europe and the Americas.
This traffic explains why about 394 boats of all nationalities were in the bay on the morning of 8 May 1902, some of them waiting for days to berth.

In the spring of 1902, Mount Pelée showed growing signs of activity (rumblings, ash falls, sulphurous gas). , a pyroclastic flow swept down the slopes of the volcano, engulfed the town in less than two minutes and reached the harbor.

The ships at anchor were struck almost simultaneously: wooden superstructures caught fire, and hulls were set ablaze or capsized by the blast and the tsunami that followed. Most vessels sank within minutes, taking their crews and cargoes with them.
Quickly buried in the mud of the harbor, some wrecks remained in a remarkable state of preservation until the first underwater explorations in the 1970s.
Archaeological research

The harbor of Saint-Pierre is now recognized for its significant archaeological value. As the former capital of Martinique, constantly frequented by a large number of ships, it preserves many traces of the past under its waters.

The University of the French Antilles has organized several excavation campaigns in collaboration with the Naval Archeology Research Group (GRAN) and the Laboratory of Medieval and Modern Archeology in the Mediterranean (LA3M).
The Department of Subaquatic and Underwater Archaeological Research (DRASSM) of the Ministry of Culture has also carried out prospecting, inventories and geophysical studies of the site.

During its various campaigns, the GRAN established a detailed list of fragments and wrecks in the bay as well as throughout Martinique. The Tamaya, the Biscaye, the Roraima and the Diamant have been definitively identified. The other wrecks have an uncertain identification.

In 2023, the ecoRoute project, co-funded by the European Union, was launched in Martinique. Led in the north of the island by the Petites Antilles Archéologie association (AAPA), it aims to promote the wrecks of Saint-Pierre and to create a tourist route around them.
Amélie / Raisinier

5 m (28 ft) wide, of 600 tons. She was built in 1890 at the Sevestre shipyard in Chantenay, on an order from the shipowners Simon and Duteil of Nantes. Having left Marseille, she arrived at Saint-Pierre at the end of April 1902.
She sprang a leak while at anchor in the harbor, the crew fought the damage for two days before she was towed to the Anse Turin by the Diamant for repairs, where she finally sank.
During its research, GRAN discovered various fragments, including the remains of an iron sailboat, badly damaged by the sea, near Raisinier beach.
The wreck lies at a depth of 12 m (39 ft). It is accessible by snorkeling.
Biscaye (ex-Gabrielle)

The Biscaye was a three-masted schooner-rigged sailing ship, built of wood with a hull lined with copper plates. It was built in Bilbao in 1878 by the Mendiguren shipyard, and measured 32 m (105 ft) long by 7 m (23 ft) wide.

Fitted out from 1895 by the Vidart et Legasse company of Bayonne, she was under the command of Captain Jules Trévty and had eight crew members. She carried cod and sugar between the Bay of Biscay, Martinique and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

Departing from Bordeaux on February 17, 1902, it reached Saint Pierre and Miquelon before arriving in Saint-Pierre, Martinique with a cargo of 700 barrels of cod on May 6. On May 8, 1902, she sank at anchor in the bay of Saint-Pierre, less than 200 m (660 ft) from the shore, facing Place Bertin.
Due to its construction, it probably caught fire quickly, unless the small tidal wave following the fiery cloud caused it to capsize and sink.

The wreck was rediscovered in the 1970s and was initially misidentified as that of the Gabrielle. The wreck measures about 31 m, while the Gabrielle measured only 23 m (75 ft 6 in). Although the Gabrielle was at anchor on May 8, she was not found.
GRAN carried out a dedicated survey of the wreck in 1994. Its dive report states the following.

The wreck of a ship, characterized by a copper-lined hull, is located practically in the axis of the Saint-Pierre pontoon. Oriented east-west, with the front facing east, it rests on a slope: the front is 29 m (95 ft) deep and the rear is 39 m (128 ft) deep.
The hull is approximately 40 m (130 ft) long. The ship is lying on its port side, clearly revealing its starboard frames and the remains of the planking with the copper sheathing.
The metal rudder, relatively well preserved, emerges one m (3 ft 3 in) from the sand. 4 in) at the top and a width of 60 cm (24 in). 1 in) below the preserved top of the rudder.
